Not on its own. The requirement is per tenant. A service-wide number could conceal a tenant below 90% of its weighted fair throughput, so the fairness check needs to retain the tenant distinction.
Does exactly 90% count for a tenant?
Yes. ‘At least 90%’ includes equality, provided the measurement is that tenant’s throughput relative to its weighted fair reference under feasible demand.
Does the activity establish that demand during the audited migrations is feasible?

It does not explicitly classify the replay’s demand. Feasible demand is a condition of the fairness requirement, so that condition must be clear when interpreting the fairness measurement. We should not assume feasibility solely from the instruction to replay migrations.
What about the below-1.2 bound—could a measured 1.2 pass?
No. ‘Below 1.2 attempts per request’ is strict. Exactly 1.2 would not meet the numerical retry-amplification bound.
Does the 10% per-tenant retry budget itself guarantee that result?

No. The 10% budget is a control in the proposal; attempts per request is the outcome the replay is meant to test. The budget percentage cannot substitute for a measured cross-replica attempts-to-requests ratio.
Should a request that crosses balancers count as a new request after migration?

For an aggregate attempts-per-request check, attempts associated with the same original logical request need to remain attributable to that request across balancers. Otherwise migration could distort the ratio. This describes what a consistent measurement requires; the activity does not specify the replay’s request-identification method.
Is the replay specifically testing request-scoped tokens instead of per-tenant retry budgets?

The activity says to test the proposed design, which specifies per-tenant 10% retry budgets. It does not explicitly select replica-local or request-scoped token accounting for this replay. We should not silently substitute one token implementation for the proposal or claim that either has been chosen here.
Can the audit cross-check decide which token approach the design uses?
No. Checking recorded grants against raw grants is an examination of the audit. It is not, by itself, a design decision about retry-token scope. That choice is not specified in this activity.
Does the replay have to keep the five-second telemetry lag?

MigFail-3 provides the migration-audit context, and the broader retry requirement specifically concerns backend failures with five-second telemetry delays. This activity does not separately state the telemetry setting for the replay. To interpret a replay result against the full retry requirement, its failure and telemetry-delay conditions would need to be explicit rather than assumed.
If the replay meets the fairness bound, can we skip the attempts-per-request measurement?
No. Fair-share attainment and retry amplification are separate outcomes. The activity explicitly tests both; a favorable fairness measurement cannot establish how many attempts were made per request.
And if attempts per request is below 1.2, does that prove every tenant is fairly served?
No. That ratio addresses retry amplification, not each tenant’s share of throughput. The replay needs a separate per-tenant fairness check.
Could the cross-check alone establish either performance bound?
No. It examines whether the audit’s token-grant records correspond to the raw grants. It does not measure tenant fair-share attainment or establish the replay’s attempts-per-request outcome.
What if a flagged grant does match a raw grant?

That would establish something about the flag’s underlying record if observed; it would not automatically establish that the grant was an improper duplicate, led to an attempt, or affected the aggregate ratio. No such cross-check finding is supplied yet.
Does this activity promise a complete explanation if one of the bounds is missed?

No. Cross-checking grants and replaying migrations can provide evidence relevant to token accounting and the two performance measures. The activity does not guarantee that those records alone will explain any measured fairness or retry outcome.
What should we record now, before the cross-check and replay produce findings?

Cross-check the MigFail-3 migration audit against raw token grants, then replay the audited migrations to test the proposed design’s at-least-90% per-tenant fairness and strictly-below-1.2 attempts-per-request bounds. Leave the audit findings, replay measurements, and threshold judgments open.
The audited MigFail-3 request-scoped replay achieved 91% minimum tenant fair-share attainment and 1.09 attempts per original request. The audit found no duplicate grants.

Those are the reported findings for the audited request-scoped replay. Its lowest measured tenant fair-share attainment was 91%, its attempts-to-original-requests ratio was 1.09, and no duplicate grants were found. The figures speak to fairness and retry amplification separately; the grant finding speaks to token accounting.
Does 91% mean every tenant in the replay attained exactly 91%?

No. It is the **minimum** tenant fair-share attainment. That means no tenant included in that measurement was reported below 91%, but it does not give the other tenants’ values or say they were equal.
How does that minimum compare with the 90% fairness threshold?

The reported minimum is one percentage point above 90%. For the tenants and conditions represented by that measurement, it clears the numerical at-least-90% level. The finding does not separately state whether demand in the replay was feasible, so that condition should remain explicit when assessing the broader requirement.
Is 1.09 the number of retries on each original request?

No. It is **attempts per original request**: a ratio of attempts to original logical requests, not 1.09 additional retries for each request. It also does not describe an identical number of attempts for every individual request.
Why retain the word “original” in that unit?

It keeps the denominator tied to the original logical requests in a migration replay. Attempts associated with a request should not become a new original request merely because handling moves between balancers. The finding reports the resulting ratio, not the individual request paths or attempt counts.
Does 1.09 satisfy the below-1.2 numerical bound?
Yes. The reported 1.09 attempts per original request is 0.11 below 1.2. That is a comparison for this audited replay, not a guarantee for every failure or migration scenario.
Can I call 1.09 the peak during the replay?
No. The finding reports 1.09 attempts per original request without identifying it as a peak, an average, or an instantaneous value. Adding “peak” would change the reported statistic.
Does “no duplicate grants” mean there were no retry tokens granted at all?
No. It says no **duplicate** grants were found. It does not say that no grants occurred, that no retries were permitted, or that every original request had just one attempt.
Does it mean a request could never receive more than one legitimate grant?

The finding does not define the grant rules or give per-request grant counts. “No duplicate grants” is the reported audit conclusion; it should not be expanded into a universal rule about how many legitimate grants a request may receive.
Can we infer that duplicate-grant flags were never generated?
No. The finding says there were no duplicate grants, not whether any audit flags were raised or how each flag was resolved. A flag and a confirmed duplicate are different things.
Does the audit finding explain every attempt included in the 1.09 ratio?

Not at the level of detail reported here. The finding supplies the ratio and says there were no duplicate grants, but it does not give an attempt-by-attempt account or attribute the measured attempts to particular token decisions.
Can I say request-scoped tokens eliminated retry amplification?

No. The reported ratio is 1.09 attempts per original request, not 1.00. The careful statement is that the audited request-scoped replay recorded 1.09 and no duplicate grants—not that additional attempts were eliminated.
Does the result prove that the whole proposed load balancer meets both requirements in all conditions?

No. It provides evidence from the audited MigFail-3 request-scoped replay: a 91% minimum tenant fair-share attainment and 1.09 attempts per original request, with no duplicate grants. It does not establish outcomes for every demand level, failure pattern, telemetry condition, or configuration of the proposed design.
What is the concise finding to record without broadening its scope?
In the audited MigFail-3 request-scoped replay, minimum tenant fair-share attainment was 91%, attempts per original request were 1.09, and the audit found no duplicate grants.

Let’s replace replica-local retry budgets with migration-safe request-scoped tokens. Local accounting reached 1.27 attempts per request; the audited tokens yielded 1.09 attempts per request and 91% fairness.

That is the decision and its stated basis. The replacement changes the scope of retry accounting from the balancer replica to the request as it moves between replicas. The cited results are 1.27 attempts per request with local accounting, versus 1.09 attempts per request and 91% fairness with the audited request-scoped tokens.
What does “migration-safe” add to “request-scoped”?

It identifies the behavior the replacement is meant to preserve when handling moves between balancer replicas: retry permission remains associated with the request rather than being treated solely as local to whichever replica handles it. The decision does not specify the token format, transfer mechanism, or accounting protocol.
Are we replacing all admission controls with tokens?

No. The decision specifically replaces replica-local **retry budgets** with migration-safe request-scoped tokens. It does not say to remove admission controls or change how backend capacity is allocated.
Does this mean the 10% retry-budget setting is retained?

The decision does not specify a percentage for the replacement tokens. It names the mechanism being replaced and the request-scoped mechanism chosen in its place. We should not infer either that the 10% setting carries over unchanged or that a new percentage has been selected.
Why is 1.27 relevant to the choice?

It is the attempts-per-request value cited for local accounting. Numerically, 1.27 is above the strictly-below-1.2 retry-amplification bound. The decision uses that contrast with the audited token result to justify replacing the replica-local approach; it does not give a further breakdown of the 1.27 value.
And how should I read 1.09?

It is the attempts-per-request result cited for the audited request-scoped tokens. Numerically, 1.09 is below 1.2. It is an observed value used to support this decision, not a guarantee that every future migration will produce exactly 1.09.
Can I say the difference is 0.18 retries per request?

The reported ratios differ by **0.18 attempts per request**: 1.27 minus 1.09. Calling that 0.18 retries per request would change the stated unit. Neither ratio describes an identical attempt count for every individual request.
Does 91% fairness mean requests were attempted 91% of the time?
No. The 91% figure is a fairness outcome; 1.09 attempts per request is the retry-amplification outcome. They measure different properties and should be reported separately.
Is 91% above the fairness threshold we care about?

Numerically, 91% is one percentage point above 90%. The decision cites that audited fairness result alongside the 1.09 attempts-per-request result. It does not turn those figures into a claim that every possible demand and failure condition has been covered.
Should I say the audited tokens guarantee every tenant 91% of its weighted fair throughput?

No. The decision states that the audited tokens yielded 91% fairness; it does not establish a universal guarantee of exactly 91% for every tenant. That would broaden a cited result into a general promise.
Does the decision say local accounting caused the fairness figure to be lower?

No. The 91% fairness figure is cited for the audited tokens, but the decision gives no corresponding fairness figure for local accounting. Its numerical contrast on retry amplification is 1.27 versus 1.09 attempts per request.
Have we established precisely why local accounting reached 1.27?

Not in this decision. It cites the 1.27 outcome as a reason for replacing replica-local budgets, but does not specify the request-level events or accounting error that produced that ratio. The replacement decision does not require us to invent such a sequence.
Can I call the request-scoped tokens a complete fix for all partial failures?

No. The decision concerns retry accounting across migration and cites the audited attempts-per-request and fairness results. It does not claim that request-scoped tokens alone resolve every aspect of partial failures or establish all load-balancer behavior.
Do request-scoped tokens mean no retries are permitted?

No. Request-scoped describes where retry permission is accounted for, not a blanket prohibition on retries. The cited 1.09 attempts per request should be stated as reported, without turning it into a no-retry claim.
What exactly should our design description change?

Where it describes retry control, it should specify **migration-safe request-scoped tokens** rather than **replica-local retry budgets**. The stated reason is that local accounting reached 1.27 attempts per request, whereas audited tokens yielded 1.09 attempts per request and 91% fairness. The decision does not add a token-issuance rule or revise unrelated controls.
Does adopting the audited approach mean its measured 1.09 value is now a configured limit?
No. The configured choice is the request-scoped token approach. The 1.09 attempts-per-request figure is a cited result, not a token limit or a parameter set to 1.09.
How should I record the choice without overstating the evidence?

Replace replica-local retry budgets with migration-safe request-scoped tokens. The decision is supported by the cited contrast—1.27 attempts per request with local accounting, versus 1.09 attempts per request and 91% fairness with audited tokens—without claiming those measured values are universal guarantees.

For the multi-tenant load balancer, I propose weighted deficit scheduling with normalized credit, 95% occupancy caps, one-second failure hysteresis, and migration-safe request-scoped retry tokens. How do those pieces fit together?

They combine tenant sharing, admission control, failure handling, and retry control. Weighted deficit scheduling with normalized credit addresses how tenants receive service according to their weights. The 95% occupancy caps constrain admitted occupancy; one-second failure hysteresis governs how failure-related control changes persist; and migration-safe request-scoped tokens keep retry accounting associated with a request as it moves between balancer replicas. This is a proposed design, not a performance result for the full combination.
What does weighted deficit scheduling contribute to fairness?

It uses tenant weights and accumulated scheduling deficits to guide service, rather than treating every tenant’s work as having an identical claim. The relevant fairness objective remains per tenant: under feasible demand, each tenant should receive at least 90% of its own weighted fair throughput. Naming the scheduler does not, by itself, demonstrate that outcome.
Why include normalized credit rather than just say weighted deficit scheduling?

Normalized credit specifies that tenant scheduling credit is retained in a form intended to remain meaningful when the amount of service available changes. That concerns the scheduler’s state, not additional backend capacity. The proposal does not provide a normalization formula or say exactly how a tenant’s balance changes at a particular event.
Does preserving normalized credit mean every tenant’s numerical deficit stays fixed?

No. Preserving credit in normalized form need not preserve every raw deficit number unchanged. The proposal identifies the property to maintain but leaves the calculation and update rules unspecified.
Are the 95% occupancy caps another way to specify the tenants’ weights?

No. Tenant weights determine the weighted fair reference used in scheduling. An occupancy cap limits the amount of work admitted under the cap’s accounting rule. The proposal does not define the denominator for 95% or say that the cap percentage is a tenant weight or fair-share entitlement.
Should I interpret 95% as the share of throughput promised to one tenant?
No. It is an occupancy-cap setting, not a promised throughput share. A tenant’s share of completed service cannot be inferred merely from that percentage.
Does a 95% cap guarantee that the remaining 5% of slots goes to other tenants?

Not from this proposal. It gives an occupancy limit but no rule reserving the remainder for a particular tenant, or even a precise definition of the capacity to which that percentage applies. Scheduling and actual admission still matter.
What is the point of combining occupancy caps with weighted scheduling?

They address different questions. Scheduling concerns which tenant should receive a service opportunity; an occupancy cap constrains how much work may occupy the capacity subject to that cap. Neither alone specifies the full behavior of the other, so the proposal includes both.
What does one-second failure hysteresis mean here?

It specifies a one-second hysteresis element in failure-related control behavior. Conceptually, hysteresis avoids treating every brief change as grounds for an immediate reversal. The proposal does not define the triggering signals, hold and release rules, or which control transitions the one-second setting governs.
Can I call that a guarantee that failures are detected within one second?
No. One-second failure hysteresis is not a stated failure-detection deadline. Nor does it establish that every limit stays fixed for exactly one second.
Is the one-second timing supposed to replace the five-second telemetry delay?

No. One second describes the proposed failure hysteresis; five seconds is the telemetry-delay condition in the retry-amplification requirement. The two timings refer to different things, and the proposal does not say that hysteresis eliminates delayed telemetry.
How do the request-scoped retry tokens help when a tenant changes balancer replicas?

Their proposed scope is the request, rather than solely the balancer currently handling it. ‘Migration-safe’ means retry permission should remain coherently associated with that request when handling moves between replicas. The proposal does not specify a token representation, transfer protocol, or number of permitted retries.
Does request-scoped mean that no request may be tried more than once?

No. Request-scoped describes how retry permission is accounted for; it does not impose a stated one-attempt-per-request rule. The desired outcome is to control aggregate attempts without assuming that every individual request has the same number of attempts.
Are these tokens still specified as a 10% per-tenant budget?

Not in this proposal. It names migration-safe request-scoped retry tokens but does not state a token-budget percentage or an issuance rule. Adding a 10% parameter here would make the proposal more specific than its wording.
What numerical retry outcome would the design need to meet?

During backend failures and five-second telemetry delays, retry amplification must stay strictly below 1.2 attempts per request. The proposed request-scoped tokens are a control aimed at that problem; their presence is not itself a measurement of the ratio.
Is exactly 1.2 attempts per request acceptable?
No. ‘Below 1.2’ excludes exactly 1.2. And the unit is total attempts per request, not 1.2 additional retries after an initial attempt.
Could the retry tokens alone establish that each tenant gets fair throughput?

No. Token accounting concerns additional attempts. Per-tenant weighted-fair throughput is a separate outcome, relevant to the weighted scheduler, normalized credit, and how admission limits affect service. A low attempts-per-request ratio would not substitute for a tenant-level fairness measurement.
Could good fairness alone show that retries are controlled?

No. Service might be distributed fairly while requests generate too many attempts. The design has to address both the at-least-90% per-tenant throughput bound under feasible demand and the strictly-below-1.2 attempts-per-request bound under the specified failure and delay conditions.
Does this proposal define the order in which scheduling, caps, hysteresis, and tokens act on a request?

No. It identifies four components to use together but does not specify a request-processing sequence, how cap decisions interact with deficit accounting, or the exact point at which a retry token is checked. Those are implementation details still to be defined.
Does one-second failure hysteresis necessarily apply to the retry tokens as well as the occupancy caps?

That relationship is not stated. Failure hysteresis and request-scoped retry tokens are both parts of the proposal, but the wording does not say that token grants follow the hysteresis timer or that the timer controls every retry decision.
Should we assume circuit breakers are included?

This proposal does not explicitly name circuit breakers. We should describe its stated components—weighted deficit scheduling with normalized credit, 95% occupancy caps, one-second failure hysteresis, and migration-safe request-scoped retry tokens—without adding an unspecified breaker rule.
Does migration safety also guarantee that the request will reach a healthy backend?
No. Migration safety here qualifies retry-token accounting across balancer replicas. It does not specify backend selection or guarantee that a particular backend can admit or complete the request.
Can high occupancy stand in for a fair-share throughput check?

No. Occupancy measures use of capacity under its own definition; weighted-fair throughput measures delivered service relative to each tenant’s weighted reference. The proposal needs both controls to work together, but it does not equate their metrics.
Is this enough detail to claim the entire design meets its requirements?

No. It is a design proposal, not an observed evaluation of the complete combination. It specifies the scheduling approach, credit treatment, occupancy-cap percentage, hysteresis duration, and retry-token scope. It does not report per-tenant throughput or attempts per request for that combined design under the required conditions.
Then give me the proposal in one sentence without implying the measurements have been made.

Use weighted deficit scheduling with normalized credit, 95% occupancy caps, one-second failure hysteresis, and migration-safe request-scoped retry tokens to pursue per-tenant fairness while controlling retry-driven load.
Can request-scoped tokens prevent duplicate retries when balancer replicas partition and receive the same request during a five-second telemetry lag?

That is an open question. Request-scoped tokens associate retry permission with a request, but a partition raises the question of whether replicas receiving the same request can recognize and enforce the same permission without coordinating. The five-second telemetry lag is part of the condition; the proposal alone does not establish that duplicate retries are prevented.
If the token belongs to the request, shouldn’t both replicas know a retry has already been authorized?

Not necessarily. Request scope describes what the permission is associated with, not what either replica can observe during a partition. Both might recognize the same request yet lack a consistent view of whether its token has been spent. Whether that can happen depends on token behavior not specified here.
What do we mean by a duplicate retry in this question?

The concern is that replicas receiving the same original request might each initiate an additional attempt when only one retry should be permitted. That is distinct from two separate original requests each receiving an authorized retry. The question does not define an exact duplicate-detection rule.
Does receiving the same request mean the replicas are definitely sending it to a backend twice?

No. Receiving the request at two replicas creates the possibility of competing decisions; it does not establish that either replica sent a retry, much less that both did. The question asks whether the tokens can prevent the duplicate outcome.
Could a request identifier alone settle it?

An identifier could help replicas recognize that they are handling the same original request. Recognition is not necessarily the same as coordinating a single retry authorization while partitioned. The question does not specify identifiers or a shared mechanism for recording token use.
So what is the crucial property the tokens would need?

Conceptually, retry permission for one original request would need to remain consistent across the replicas that receive it, so that one permitted retry cannot be spent independently by each. That states the property at issue, not a chosen implementation or proof that it holds during a partition.
Is ‘migration-safe’ enough to imply that property?

No. Accounting for a request as it moves between replicas is not automatically the same as handling two replicas that receive the same request while unable to coordinate. This question asks whether request-scoped tokens also address that partition case; it does not establish that they do.
Does the five-second telemetry lag cause the partition?

No causal link is stated. The partition and the five-second telemetry lag are conditions in the question. Delayed telemetry may limit how current feedback is, but it does not tell us why the replicas partitioned or what information they can exchange.
Could telemetry arriving after five seconds tell the replicas in time not to issue a duplicate retry?

The question does not establish that. A later update might reveal information after decisions have already been made, but no decision timing or telemetry contents are specified. Preventing a duplicate retry is different from discovering one afterward.
Does preventing duplicate retries mean prohibiting every retry?

No. The question is about avoiding *duplicate* retry decisions for the same request across partitioned replicas. It does not call for eliminating all retries, or say how many legitimate attempts an individual request may receive.
If each replica stays within a retry budget, could duplicate retries still occur?

Conceptually, yes. Separate local compliance would not by itself tell us whether both replicas spent permission on the same original request. Request-scoped tokens are meant to focus accounting on that request, but their behavior during a partition remains the unresolved issue.
Could we infer that a duplicate happened just because two replicas logged the same request?

No. Those records would show that both received the request, not that both sent additional attempts. To identify a duplicate retry, the attempt decisions would have to be related to the same original request. No such observations are reported in this question.
What if one replica considers its token spent and the other has no record of that?

That illustrates the uncertainty: request-scoped accounting would need to prevent the second replica from independently treating the same permission as available. The question does not say that this split view actually occurs or specify how the tokens behave if it does.
Can we simply require the replicas to agree before any retry?

That would be a possible design rule to consider, not a requirement or decision stated here. The question provides no coordination protocol or policy for a replica that cannot reach another during a partition. We should not present one as the existing token behavior.
Does ‘prevent’ require that no duplicate retry ever happens in the partition scenario?

In this question, prevention concerns whether the tokens stop replicas from making duplicate retries for the same request under the stated partition and five-second lag. No probability, exception allowance, or measurement window is specified, so we should not replace that question with a weaker numerical claim.
How is this different from asking whether attempts per request stays below 1.2?

Duplicate-retry prevention concerns whether the same request receives independently authorized additional attempts across replicas. Attempts per request is an aggregate ratio. A ratio alone would not identify duplicate decisions, and avoiding one duplicate would not, by itself, establish the aggregate bound during backend failures and five-second telemetry delays.
Could the aggregate ratio be below 1.2 even if some duplicate retries occur?

In principle, yes: a ratio across requests can conceal what happened to particular requests. Conversely, an absence of duplicate retries across replicas would not establish that all other retry activity keeps the ratio below 1.2. The question focuses specifically on duplicates in the partitioned-replica case.
Does the question specify how many replicas partition or how many requests they both receive?

No. It says balancer replicas partition and receive the same request, but does not give a replica count, request count, partition duration, or pattern of delivery. Those quantities should remain unspecified.
Can we use a prior migration result as proof for this case?

No. The present question concerns simultaneous handling of the same request by partitioned replicas under a five-second telemetry lag. The wording does not supply a result for that condition, so the ability of request-scoped tokens to prevent duplicate retries remains to be determined.
What would we have to distinguish to answer it carefully?

We would need to distinguish receipt of the same original request by multiple replicas, authorization of a retry, and an attempt actually being sent. We would also need to know whether token expenditure for that request can be recognized consistently despite the partition. The question specifies none of those observations or implementation rules.
So what is the precise unresolved question?

Whether migration-safe, request-scoped retry permission can be enforced once per original request when partitioned balancer replicas both receive it, preventing duplicate retries despite five-second-late telemetry. The current question states the challenge, not its answer.
My hypothesis is that partitioned balancer replicas can each redeem request-scoped tokens without shared state, raising attempts per original request above 1.2 despite the token limits.

That proposes a specific failure mode, not an observed result. Even though retry tokens are scoped to a request, partitioned replicas receiving that request might each redeem permission without knowing that another replica has done so. The predicted outcome is an attempts-per-original-request ratio strictly above 1.2, despite the token limits.
Isn’t “request-scoped” supposed to mean there is only one token for the request?

Request scope identifies which request the retry permission belongs to. By itself, it does not establish that redemption is coordinated across replicas that cannot share state. The hypothesis is precisely that a request-scoped limit might be enforced separately at those replicas during a partition.
So are you claiming that the request is assigned two different identities?

No. The proposed problem could arise even if both replicas recognize the same original request: each may be unable to see the other’s redemption. The hypothesis does not say that request identities change or specify how the tokens are represented.
What does “without shared state” mean for this claim?

It means the replicas cannot rely on a common, current record of whether retry permission for that request has already been redeemed. The hypothesis connects that absence to the possibility of independent redemptions. It does not specify whether shared state is absent permanently or only while the replicas are partitioned.
Is the hypothesis that every partitioned replica definitely redeems a token?

No. “Can each redeem” expresses a possible behavior under the stated conditions, not a claim that every replica always does so. The hypothesis predicts that this behavior can push the aggregate attempts-per-original-request measure above 1.2; it gives neither a count of redemptions nor a frequency.
Does redeeming a token necessarily mean an attempt was sent?

The proposed causal chain connects independent token redemptions to additional attempts, but a redemption event and a sent attempt are conceptually distinct. The hypothesis does not provide event records showing that every redemption produced an attempt. Its predicted metric is attempts per original request, which would need to be assessed from attempts rather than inferred merely from token use.
What makes the attempts-per-request number aggregate rather than replica-local?

The denominator is original requests, and the numerator must include attempts attributable to them even when those attempts occur at different replicas. Counting each replica’s own attempts in isolation could miss the cross-replica effect the hypothesis describes. No counting window or aggregation rule is supplied here.
Why is the word “original” important?

The same original request may be received by more than one partitioned replica. It should not become multiple original requests in the denominator just because its handling is duplicated. The hypothesized excess concerns additional attempts associated with those original requests.
Does above 1.2 mean exactly 1.2 would confirm the hypothesis?

No. “Above 1.2 attempts per original request” is strict: exactly 1.2 would not match this prediction. The broader retry requirement says *below* 1.2 attempts per request under its stated conditions, so equality would not satisfy that requirement either.
Could I call that 1.2 additional retries for each original request?

No. The stated unit is total attempts per original request, not additional retries per original request. It is also a ratio across the requests considered; it does not describe an identical number of attempts on every individual request.
If only one original request gets duplicate attempts, must the aggregate exceed 1.2?

Not necessarily. An aggregate ratio depends on the attempts and original requests across the population being measured. The hypothesis predicts an above-1.2 outcome under the partitioned-replica behavior, but a duplicate retry for a single request alone would not establish that aggregate threshold.
Does this imply that token limits are completely ineffective?

No. The claim is narrower: token limits may fail to constrain *cross-replica redemption for the same request* when replicas are partitioned and lack shared state. The hypothesis does not say the limits never constrain retries or describe all other circumstances.
Can each replica comply with what it sees locally while this problem occurs?

That is the proposed tension. Each replica might treat a redemption as permitted under its local view, while the combined attempts attributable to original requests exceed the intended aggregate bound. This is a possible explanation, not a finding that any replica actually complied locally or that the aggregate bound was exceeded.
Does a partition itself create retry tokens?
No such mechanism is stated. The proposed risk is independent redemption of request-scoped permission without shared state, not that partitioning creates tokens or backend capacity.
Do we know how many replicas receive the same request?
No number is given. The hypothesis refers to partitioned replicas and the same request, but it does not specify a replica count, how many requests are duplicated, or how long the partition lasts.
Is the five-second telemetry lag the reason the replicas cannot share state?

The surrounding question places this scenario during a five-second telemetry lag, but the hypothesis attributes the possible independent redemptions to the absence of shared state across partitioned replicas. It does not say the telemetry lag causes the partition or defines what information a telemetry update contains.
Would a telemetry update five seconds later undo an attempt already made?

No later update should be assumed to undo an attempt. The hypothesis is about preventing independent redemptions before they produce an aggregate attempts-per-original-request ratio above 1.2. It does not specify when any update arrives relative to a particular redemption or attempt.
Are backend failures explicitly part of this hypothesis?

The hypothesis itself names partitioned replicas, request-scoped token redemption without shared state, token limits, and an above-1.2 attempts-per-original-request outcome. Its surrounding question specifies a five-second telemetry lag. It does not supply a backend-failure pattern, so the proposed outcome should not be presented as a measurement under a particular backend failure.
Can we conclude request-scoped tokens are unsafe whenever replicas partition?

No. This is a conditional failure-mode hypothesis, not a universal conclusion. It proposes that replicas *can* each redeem without shared state and that the resulting attempts per original request can exceed 1.2. Whether a given token mechanism permits that behavior remains to be determined.
What would distinguish observing the proposed mechanism from observing only an above-1.2 ratio?

The ratio would describe the aggregate amplification outcome. To identify the proposed mechanism specifically, one would have to relate the same original request to token redemptions at partitioned replicas and to any attempts those redemptions permit. An above-1.2 ratio by itself would not establish that independent redemption caused it.
And if two replicas redeem for the same request, does that alone prove the ratio exceeds 1.2?

No. Such redemptions, if observed, would bear on the proposed mechanism, but the aggregate ratio still depends on attempts actually made and the original-request population. The hypothesis links these propositions; neither can be substituted for a measurement of the other.
How should I phrase the claim while keeping both parts hypothetical?

“Hypothesis: when partitioned balancer replicas receive the same request without shared state, each can redeem request-scoped retry permission; despite token limits, the resulting aggregate attempts per original request may rise strictly above 1.2.”
Let’s partition the MigFail-3 balancers for five seconds, replay duplicate request IDs, and compare independent token redemption against single-writer leases.

That is a plan to test how retry permission behaves when balancers cannot coordinate. The five-second partition and duplicate request IDs create the comparison setting. Independent token redemption and single-writer leases are the two approaches to compare. The plan does not report redemptions, duplicate retries, or attempts per original request.
Why replay duplicate request IDs?

They let the comparison focus on balancers handling what is identified as the same request. That makes it possible to ask whether retry permission is independently redeemed for one request during the partition. The plan does not say how many IDs are replayed or how often each appears.
Does a duplicate request ID prove that a duplicate retry was sent?

No. An ID appearing at more than one balancer concerns request receipt or representation. A duplicate retry would require additional attempt decisions for that same original request. The replay is intended to examine that possibility, not presume it.
What does independent token redemption mean in this comparison?

Conceptually, it means a balancer can redeem retry permission without first relying on a shared, current decision by another balancer. That is the behavior being compared under the partition. The plan does not specify a token format, how many tokens exist, or how a redemption leads to an attempt.
And what is the contrasting idea behind a single-writer lease?

It is to designate one writer for a request’s retry-permission decisions for the duration governed by the lease, rather than allow independent decisions at multiple balancers. The plan does not specify how a writer is selected, how long a lease lasts, or what a balancer does if it cannot reach that writer.
Is the lease duration five seconds?

That is not stated. Five seconds is the planned duration of the balancer partition. The lease duration and its renewal or expiry rules are unspecified, so they should not be equated with the partition duration.
Does single-writer mean exactly one balancer receives the request?

No. Duplicate request IDs are being replayed precisely to examine handling of the same request across balancers. A single writer would concern who may make the relevant token-redemption decision, not necessarily which balancers can receive the request.
Are we proposing to use leases permanently?

Not in this node. The plan compares independent redemption with single-writer leases in the five-second partition setting. It does not select either approach for the load balancer or state how it would be deployed.
Does the five-second partition imply that telemetry is also delayed by exactly five seconds?

The plan explicitly specifies a five-second balancer partition. The motivating question also concerns a five-second telemetry lag, but the plan does not separately state a telemetry-delay setting for this replay. A partition and a telemetry lag are different conditions; their equal numerical duration would not make them interchangeable.
Can I assume the partition starts when a backend fails?

No. The plan does not specify a backend failure event or the partition’s trigger. MigFail-3 identifies the setting to partition, but this instruction adds no event timeline connecting backend failure, request replay, and partition onset.
Do all three MigFail-3 balancers have to be separated from one another?

The plan says to partition the MigFail-3 balancers, but does not specify the partition topology. It does not say which balancers can still communicate or exactly which receive each duplicate request ID.
What observation would make the comparison relevant to duplicate retries?

We would want to distinguish receipt of a duplicate ID, redemption of retry permission for that ID, and an additional attempt actually sent for its original request. Comparing those events under independent redemption and single-writer leases would address duplicate-retry behavior. The plan does not specify the logs or provide any such observations yet.
If two balancers independently redeem a token, is that automatically two backend attempts?

No. Redemption and an actual attempt are distinct events. Two redemptions for the same request, if observed, would bear on the proposed accounting problem, but the attempt outcome would still need to be established separately.
Would a single-writer lease necessarily stop every retry during the partition?

Not necessarily. The proposed contrast is between independent redemption and a single designated writer, not between retries and no retries. The plan leaves open whether the lease holder can authorize a retry and how other balancers behave when they cannot contact it.
Could a replica that loses access to the writer simply issue its own lease?

The plan gives no lease-acquisition rule, so we cannot assume that behavior or rule it out as an implementation fact. Whether the single-writer property remains enforceable throughout the partition is part of what the comparison would need to make clear.
Is a five-second partition enough by itself to show token double-spending?

No. It provides a condition in which shared-state assumptions can be tested. It does not establish that either approach redeems permission twice for the same request or that additional attempts result.
Should we expect the lease approach to keep aggregate attempts per original request below 1.2?

That would be a possible outcome to examine, not a result of the plan. This node specifies a comparison of redemption approaches but does not explicitly call for an attempts-per-original-request measurement or predict a ratio for either approach.
Then does the plan directly test the 1.2 threshold?

Not as written. Its stated actions are a five-second partition, a replay of duplicate request IDs, and a comparison of independent token redemption with single-writer leases. To judge the numerical amplification bound, attempts and original requests would also have to be measured on a defined basis. The present plan reports no such measurement.
Could single-writer leases avoid duplicate grants but still affect service?

Conceptually, enforcing one writer could change when a balancer is able to decide about retry permission during a partition. That does not establish what happens to service, latency, or fairness here. The plan does not request those measurements or predict an effect.
Does a lease result tell us whether each tenant attains at least 90% of weighted fair throughput?

No. Retry-token redemption and per-tenant fair-share throughput are different questions. This comparison does not specify a fair-share attainment measurement, so it cannot by itself establish the per-tenant 90% requirement.
What should we avoid claiming until the replay is examined?

We should not claim that independent redemption produced duplicate retries, that leases prevented them, or that either approach met the below-1.2 attempts-per-request bound. The plan gives the conditions and approaches to compare, but no observations or outcome.
Can you restate the plan precisely?

Partition the MigFail-3 balancers for five seconds, replay duplicate request IDs, and compare independent token redemption against single-writer leases. Keep the partition duration distinct from any unstated lease duration or telemetry setting, and leave the comparison’s results open.
Run PartitionMig-5 with duplicate request IDs across partitioned balancers and a five-second lag. Record token redemptions and attempts per original request.

That defines the PartitionMig-5 activity. It places duplicate request IDs at partitioned balancers under a five-second lag and calls for two observations: token redemptions and attempts per original request. No redemption pattern or attempts-per-original-request value is reported yet.
What is this run trying to distinguish?

It separates a question about retry permission from a question about attempts actually made. The redemption records can show what happened to tokens for requests seen across partitioned balancers. Attempts per original request measures the resulting amplification across those requests. Neither observation should be inferred from the other before the records are examined.
Does a duplicate request ID mean the system has two original requests?

No. In this run, duplicate IDs are used to examine handling of what is identified as the same request across balancers. For attempts per *original* request, receiving that ID at another balancer must not automatically add another original request to the denominator.
Does it prove both balancers issued a retry?
No. Receiving duplicate request IDs does not establish that either balancer redeemed a token or sent an additional attempt. Those are the behaviors PartitionMig-5 is intended to observe.
Why log redemptions as well as the aggregate attempts ratio?

An attempts-per-original-request value would tell us how much amplification was measured, but not whether separate balancers redeemed retry permission for the same request. Redemption records bear on that proposed mechanism. Conversely, a redemption record alone would not establish how many attempts were sent across the original requests.
If I see two redemptions for the same ID, can I immediately count two retries?

No. A redemption of retry permission and an attempt actually sent are distinct events. Two redemptions for one ID would be relevant to examining independent token use, if observed, but the attempts measurement is still needed to establish the effect on attempts per original request.
And if attempts per original request exceeds 1.2, does that prove both balancers redeemed the same token?

No. A ratio above 1.2 would establish a numerical amplification outcome on its measurement basis, not its cause. To connect that outcome to cross-balancer redemption, the redemption records would need to show the relevant behavior for the same original requests.
Is above 1.2 what PartitionMig-5 is expected to produce?

That is a hypothesis this run can examine, not a result specified by the activity. PartitionMig-5 calls for recording redemptions and attempts per original request; it does not predict a value or say the token limits will be exceeded.
What does the five-second lag refer to here?

The motivating question concerns five-second telemetry lag while balancer replicas are partitioned. PartitionMig-5 specifies that five-second lag as a run condition. It does not give a telemetry update schedule or say at which point in the lag any particular redemption occurs.
Does that also mean the partition lasts exactly five seconds?

The activity says the balancers are partitioned *with a five-second lag*; it does not explicitly give a partition duration. A lag duration and a partition duration are different quantities, so I would not equate them in the description of this run.
How many balancers receive each duplicate ID?
The activity does not specify a number for each ID. It says duplicate request IDs occur across partitioned balancers, but gives neither the partition topology nor a per-request delivery pattern.
Does the name PartitionMig-5 tell us the number of balancers or migrations?
No. PartitionMig-5 is the run name. The activity does not define what the ‘5’ denotes, and it supplies no count of balancers, migrations, or duplicate IDs.
Are these necessarily backend-failure retries?

The activity does not specify a backend-failure pattern. It focuses on partitioned balancers receiving duplicate request IDs under a five-second lag. We should not add particular backend failures or causes for the duplicate delivery.
What would a token-redemption record need to retain to be useful for this question?

It would need to make redemptions attributable to the original request and to the balancer making each redemption, so cross-balancer behavior for the same ID can be examined. That describes the distinction the investigation needs; the activity does not prescribe a record format or report any such events.
Could the balancers both receive an ID but only one redeem a token?
That is possible in principle. Duplicate receipt and duplicate redemption are separate. PartitionMig-5 is meant to observe what happens rather than presume that both balancers act identically.
Is attempts per original request the same thing as retries per request?

No. Attempts per original request counts attempts relative to original logical requests, not only retries after an initial attempt. The resulting ratio also would not imply that every individual request had an identical number of attempts.
Would exactly 1.2 match the hypothesis that amplification rises above 1.2?

No. ‘Above 1.2’ excludes equality. The broader retry requirement is ‘below 1.2 attempts per request’ during backend failures and five-second telemetry delays, which also excludes equality. PartitionMig-5 provides no measured ratio yet, and it does not explicitly specify backend failures.
Is the run explicitly comparing independent redemption with single-writer leases?

That comparison motivates the work, but this PartitionMig-5 activity specifically names duplicate request IDs, partitioned balancers, a five-second lag, and the two quantities to record. It does not explicitly identify which redemption approach or approaches are enabled in the run, so I would not report a lease-versus-independent result from the activity description alone.
Can the run by itself establish that the complete load balancer meets its fairness target?

No. It does not call for tenant fair-share attainment measurements. Weighted scheduling, normalized credit, occupancy caps, and failure hysteresis are not evaluated merely by recording token redemptions and attempts per original request.
Would an absence of duplicate redemptions establish that attempts stayed below 1.2?

No. Avoiding duplicate redemption across balancers would address one possible source of extra attempts. Other attempts could still affect the ratio. The recorded attempts-per-original-request value is needed to assess amplification; no such value is given yet.
What is the faithful record of PartitionMig-5 before we inspect its output?

Run PartitionMig-5 with duplicate request IDs across partitioned balancers and a five-second lag, recording token redemptions and attempts per original request. Leave open whether the same request receives independent redemptions and what amplification the run measures.
PartitionMig-5 reports that independent redemption duplicated 4% of retry tokens, but attempts per request stayed at 1.17. Minimum tenant fair-share attainment fell to 85%.

That gives three distinct findings for PartitionMig-5: independent redemption duplicated 4% of retry tokens; the reported attempts-per-request value stayed at 1.17 despite that duplication; and the minimum tenant fair-share attainment fell to 85%. The token finding, attempt ratio, and fairness outcome should not be treated as interchangeable measures.
Does 4% mean that 4% of requests received duplicate retries?

No. The reported percentage is of **retry tokens** duplicated by independent redemption, not of requests. The result does not say how many requests were affected or how many additional attempts the duplicated tokens produced.
But does this establish that independent redemption actually duplicated tokens, rather than merely risking it?

Yes. In PartitionMig-5, duplication of 4% of retry tokens is reported as an observed result of independent redemption. That finding should remain specific to this run; it does not give a duplication rate for other partition conditions.
Can I equate each duplicated token with one extra backend attempt?

No. A token redemption and an attempt actually made are different events. The result reports token duplication and an attempts-per-request ratio, but does not provide a token-by-token account showing which duplicate redemptions led to attempts.
How should I understand the word “but” between the duplication and the 1.17 figure?

It highlights that token duplication occurred while the reported attempts-per-request value nevertheless stayed at 1.17. It does not mean the duplicates had no effect on attempts, or that we know what the ratio would have been without duplication.
Is 1.17 the peak attempts-per-request value during the partition?

The finding does not call 1.17 a peak. It says attempts per request stayed at 1.17, without specifying a measurement window or a peak statistic. I would retain that wording rather than add a qualifier.
Does 1.17 mean each request was attempted exactly 1.17 times?
No. Attempts per request is a ratio across requests, not an identical attempt count for each individual request. The result provides no distribution of attempts among requests.
Could I calculate the share of requests retried from 1.17?

Not uniquely. The same attempts-per-request ratio can arise from different distributions of additional attempts across requests. PartitionMig-5 does not report how many requests were retried or how often any one request was attempted.
The run used duplicate request IDs across partitioned balancers. Does the finding say every duplicate ID produced a duplicated token?

No. The setup involved duplicate request IDs across partitioned balancers, while the finding reports that 4% of retry tokens were duplicated under independent redemption. It does not give a per-ID breakdown or say that every duplicated ID resulted in duplicate redemption.
Was the five-second lag part of the reported setting?

Yes. PartitionMig-5 was run with a five-second lag and duplicate request IDs across partitioned balancers. The finding does not specify when within that lag the token duplications or fairness decline occurred.
Does the five-second lag tell us how long the balancers were partitioned?
Not from this result. The five-second lag is stated for the run, but this finding gives no separate partition duration or sequence of partition events.
What does “minimum tenant fair-share attainment fell to 85%” establish?

It establishes that the reported lowest tenant fair-share attainment was 85%, and that this was a decline. It does not identify the tenant, give the earlier attainment value from which it fell, or report the other tenants’ attainments.
Can I say every tenant’s attainment fell to 85%?
No. Eighty-five percent is the **minimum**. Other tenants’ attainment values are not supplied, and the finding does not say they declined by the same amount.
Does the 85% figure tell us whether backend slots were idle?

No. Fair-share attainment compares a tenant’s service with its weighted fair reference. It is not a slot-occupancy measure. PartitionMig-5 does not report occupancy or slot assignments in this finding.
Could duplicated retry tokens have caused the fairness decline?

That is a possible question to investigate, but the reported numbers do not establish a causal link. We know duplication occurred and the minimum attainment fell to 85%; we do not know whether the duplicated tokens affected that tenant’s service or what else contributed to the decline.
Could I instead say the attempt ratio caused the decline?

No. The 1.17 attempts-per-request figure and the 85% minimum attainment are concurrent reported outcomes, not a causal explanation of one another. The result does not show which attempts affected which tenant’s throughput.
Does this finding report what happened with single-writer leases?
No. The reported token-duplication result is for **independent redemption**. This finding gives no token-duplication, attempts-per-request, or fairness result for a single-writer-lease condition.
Can we conclude that request-scoped tokens always duplicate 4% of grants in a partition?
No. The 4% figure is specific to the independent-redemption behavior reported in PartitionMig-5. The finding does not establish a universal rate for request-scoped tokens or for other partitions.
Does the result specify which tenant weights or occupancy-cap setting were in use?

No. It reports token duplication, attempts per request, and the minimum tenant fair-share attainment, but does not state tenant weights or an occupancy-cap setting for this result. Those details should not be inferred.
How would you record these findings without guessing at the fairness cause or a lease outcome?

In PartitionMig-5, independent redemption duplicated 4% of retry tokens, while attempts per request stayed at 1.17; minimum tenant fair-share attainment fell to 85%. The finding does not identify the cause of the fairness decline or report a single-writer-lease result.
Let’s defer the proposed load-balancer design for now. Retain request-scoped retry tokens, but diagnose and correct PartitionMig-5’s 85% tenant fair-share attainment.

Understood. The decision defers the full proposal while keeping request-scoped retry tokens. The unresolved work is to determine why PartitionMig-5 produced 85% tenant fair-share attainment and address that outcome. This does not identify its cause or claim that a correction has already worked.
Does deferring the proposal mean we’re dropping request-scoped tokens too?
No. Retaining request-scoped tokens is an explicit part of the decision. Deferring the full proposal and keeping that retry-control component are compatible.
Does it mean the rest of the proposal has been rejected?
No. “Defer” means the proposal is not being taken forward as a complete design at this point. It does not, by itself, reject each of its other components or choose replacements for them.
What is the specific problem we’re pausing to address?

PartitionMig-5’s reported 85% tenant fair-share attainment. The decision calls for diagnosing why that outcome occurred and correcting it, rather than assuming the proposed design can be adopted without addressing it.
Do we already know why the tenant reached 85%?
No cause is specified in this decision. Diagnosis remains work to be done; attributing the 85% to a particular control or failure mechanism now would be premature.
Should we change the retry tokens as part of that diagnosis?

The decision says to retain request-scoped retry tokens. It does not prescribe a token change as the correction for fair-share attainment. Diagnosis should not be mistaken for a decision about which component must change.
Does retaining them prove that they can prevent every duplicate retry?

No. Retaining request-scoped tokens is a design decision, not a universal guarantee about every partition or retry decision. This decision’s stated reason for deferring the full proposal is the 85% tenant fair-share outcome; it makes no new claim about duplicate-retry prevention.
Is 85% an occupancy figure?
No. It is tenant fair-share attainment—a measure of tenant service relative to its weighted fair reference. It should not be relabeled as backend occupancy or as a percentage of requests retried.
Can we call a correction successful just because more slots are occupied?

Not on that basis alone. The outcome identified for correction is tenant fair-share attainment. Slot occupancy, if considered, would be a different measure; it would not by itself show that the 85% attainment issue has been corrected.
What does “diagnose and correct” commit us to, without choosing an unsupported fix?

It commits to identifying the reason for the PartitionMig-5 fairness outcome and addressing that reason. It does not specify a corrective mechanism, a new attainment value, or a completed test of a fix.
Could we simply rename the 85% result as a temporary dip and proceed?

The decision does not classify the 85% result as temporary or authorize setting it aside. It expressly calls for diagnosing and correcting that fair-share attainment while the full proposal is deferred.
Does this decision set a deadline or a particular experiment for the diagnosis?
No. It identifies the work and the observed 85% outcome, but does not specify a deadline, an experiment, or an instrumentation method. Those details remain open.
What should our current design-status statement avoid claiming?

It should not claim that the full proposal has been adopted, that the 85% fairness issue has a known cause, or that a correction has already restored attainment. It should also not imply that request-scoped tokens were discarded.
Give me the decision in a single sentence.
Defer the full proposed design, retain request-scoped retry tokens, and diagnose and correct PartitionMig-5’s 85% tenant fair-share attainment.

For the multi-tenant load balancer, I propose partition-stable tenant capacity reservations with local borrowing, normalized deficit accounting, and deterministic request-owner retry fencing. How do those pieces work together?

They address three related concerns. Partition-stable tenant capacity reservations provide a tenant-level capacity allocation intended to remain meaningful when balancer replicas partition. Local borrowing allows available reserved capacity to be used rather than necessarily left idle. Normalized deficit accounting tracks tenant service relative to the scheduling framework, while deterministic request-owner retry fencing addresses which replica may authorize a retry for a given request. This is a proposal, not a measured result for the combined design.
What does “partition-stable” mean for a reservation?

It expresses the intended property that a tenant’s capacity reservation remains well defined across a replica partition, rather than depending on an immediate shared update that partitioned replicas cannot obtain. The proposal does not specify how reservations are represented, assigned among replicas, or reconciled when communication returns.
Does that mean each tenant has a guaranteed throughput regardless of capacity?

No. A capacity reservation is not a claim that service can be delivered without sufficient capacity. The broader fairness objective applies under feasible demand: each tenant should receive at least 90% of its weighted fair throughput. The proposal does not establish that outcome under every capacity condition.
Is a tenant’s reservation necessarily equal to its weighted fair throughput?

That equality is not specified. Reservations concern allocated capacity, while weighted fair throughput is a reference for evaluating delivered tenant service. The proposal does not give reservation sizes or a formula linking them to tenant weights.
Why have reservations at all if the scheduler tracks deficits?

They serve distinct purposes. A reservation concerns capacity available for a tenant; deficit accounting concerns how tenant service is tracked for scheduling. Tracking that a tenant is owed service does not, by itself, ensure that capacity is available to serve it during a partition. Conversely, reserving capacity does not specify how accumulated scheduling credit should be accounted for.
What does “local borrowing” add to the reservation idea?

It allows capacity associated with a reservation to be used locally when the reserving tenant is not using it, subject to whatever borrowing rule is eventually specified. The proposal does not define eligibility, how much may be borrowed, or how borrowed capacity is returned to its reserved tenant.
Could borrowing make the reservation meaningless?

That is a design question the borrowing rule would need to address. The proposal calls for both partition-stable reservations and local borrowing, so borrowing should not be described as simply abolishing reservations. But the wording does not establish how the two are enforced together or prove that borrowing leaves the intended tenant capacity available when needed.
Does local borrowing mean a tenant permanently transfers its reservation to another tenant?

No permanent transfer is stated. “Borrowing” indicates use of capacity associated with another reservation, but the proposal does not specify its duration or the conditions for ending it. Treating borrowed capacity as permanently reassigned would add a decision that is not present.
Is borrowing necessarily between balancer replicas?

The word “local” signals that the borrowing decision is local, but the proposal does not identify the precise locality boundary or prescribe a cross-replica transfer. It is safer to keep the description at the stated level than to invent a mechanism for moving capacity between replicas.
Could two partitioned replicas each borrow the same capacity?

That is a question the eventual reservation and borrowing rules would need to resolve. Partition stability is an intended property, but the proposal supplies no capacity-accounting protocol from which to determine whether double allocation is possible or prevented.
What does normalized deficit accounting mean in this combination?

It means tracking tenant scheduling deficits in a normalized form so that the accounting remains interpretable as capacity availability and service change. The proposal does not state the normalization basis, update formula, or exactly how reserved versus borrowed service affects a tenant’s balance.
Does normalization set each tenant’s deficit to zero when a partition occurs?
No such reset rule is specified. Normalized accounting identifies the form of the deficit state, not a requirement to erase accumulated credit on a partition or on a slot change.
Would borrowed service count toward the borrower’s deficit, the reservation owner’s deficit, or both?

The proposal does not settle that accounting rule. It is an important distinction: capacity ownership and the tenant that actually receives service need not be the same when borrowing is allowed. The rule would have to be made explicit before a fair-share measurement could be interpreted against the accounting.
Why is it important not to infer that rule?

Because the fairness objective concerns service delivered to each tenant relative to its weighted fair throughput. Charging or crediting borrowed service to a different tenant would change what the deficit state represents. The proposal names normalized deficit accounting, but provides no specific attribution rule to report as fact.
Now what is a deterministic request owner?

It is a way of identifying one owner for retry decisions associated with a particular request, with the intended property that the owner is determined consistently. The proposal does not say how ownership is computed, where the decision is stored, or how a replica reaches the owner during a partition.
Does deterministic ownership mean only one replica can receive the request?

No. Receiving a request and being authorized to make its retry decision are different matters. Request-owner retry fencing concerns the latter. The proposal does not restrict delivery of a request to a single replica.
What does “fencing” contribute beyond choosing an owner?

Fencing expresses the intended exclusion of retry decisions made outside the authorized request owner. Determining an owner and enforcing that boundary are distinct: an ownership rule alone would not show what happens when another replica receives the request. The proposal does not define the enforcement mechanism.
Is the owner necessarily the replica that handled the initial attempt?
No ownership rule of that kind is given. The proposal says the owner is deterministic, not that it is the first replica to see the request or that ownership never changes.
If a replica cannot contact the request owner during a partition, what does it do?

The proposal does not specify that behavior. Answering would require a policy for an unreachable owner, including whether a retry waits, is declined, or is handled in some other way. None of those responses should be treated as chosen here.
Would fencing prevent every duplicate request from reaching a backend?

The stated fencing concerns retries and request ownership. It should not be expanded into a guarantee about every duplicate delivery or every initial attempt. Whether the proposed fencing prevents duplicate retries under a particular partition condition requires a defined mechanism and observations.
Does deterministic fencing eliminate the need to measure attempts per request?

No. Fencing is a proposed control, whereas attempts per request is an outcome. During backend failures and five-second telemetry delays, the broader requirement is strictly below 1.2 attempts per request. The name of a control cannot establish that measured bound.
Could a request still be retried legitimately under this proposal?

Yes, the wording does not prohibit all retries. It proposes fencing retry decisions to a deterministic request owner. It does not specify how many retries that owner may authorize or the conditions for authorization.
Does the proposal include a retry-budget percentage?

No. It specifies deterministic request-owner retry fencing but does not give a retry-budget percentage, token allowance, or attempts-per-request setting. Adding any of those as a component of this proposal would go beyond its content.
How do reservations and retry fencing interact?

They concern different resources and decisions. Reservations and local borrowing concern tenant access to capacity; request-owner fencing concerns authorization of additional attempts for a request. A retry can affect offered load, so both matter to a load balancer, but the proposal does not specify the order in which capacity admission and retry authorization occur.
Could an authorized retry automatically use another tenant’s reserved capacity?

That is not stated. Retry authorization does not itself determine which capacity may admit the resulting attempt. The borrowing and admission rules would need to specify whether such use is allowed; the proposal does not.
Is the reservation per tenant or per request?

The proposal explicitly calls for *tenant capacity reservations*. Retry fencing, in contrast, is scoped to a request owner. Keeping those scopes distinct avoids treating a request’s retry permission as an entitlement to another tenant’s reserved capacity.
How would we know whether local borrowing preserves fairness?

We would need to compare delivered throughput for each tenant with its own weighted fair throughput under feasible demand. The target is at least 90% per tenant. Neither the existence of a reservation nor the use of borrowed capacity, by itself, supplies those throughput measurements.
Would high utilization of reserved and borrowed capacity be sufficient evidence?

No. Utilization concerns how much capacity is used; fairness concerns which tenants receive service relative to their weighted fair references. High utilization can coexist with an uneven tenant allocation, so the measures should not be conflated.
Could the fencing keep retries low but reduce a tenant’s throughput?

That is a possible trade-off to examine, not an effect reported for this proposal. Preventing an unauthorized retry and delivering fair throughput are separate questions. The proposed combination would need to be judged on both, rather than assuming success on one establishes success on the other.
Does the proposal say what happens when a reservation’s tenant has no demand?

It includes local borrowing, which suggests a way capacity might be used rather than left idle, but it does not specify when a reservation counts as available to borrow or how lack of demand is determined. A precise idle-capacity rule is not supplied.
Could a borrowed slot be reclaimed instantly when its reserving tenant needs it?
No reclamation timing is specified. Instant reclamation would be an additional implementation commitment, not something implied by the phrase “local borrowing.”
Does ‘partition-stable’ promise that each replica knows the current total backend capacity?

No. Stability of tenant reservations during a partition is not the same as perfect knowledge of changing backend capacity. The proposal does not describe telemetry, capacity discovery, or how reservation amounts respond to partial backend failures.
Can I say this proposal already handles five-second telemetry delays?

It is proposed for a load balancer whose retry requirement includes five-second telemetry delays, but the proposal does not provide a measured outcome or a detailed telemetry-handling rule. It should not be presented as having already demonstrated performance during that delay.
What would a faithful one-sentence description be?

Use partition-stable tenant capacity reservations with local borrowing, normalized deficit accounting, and deterministic request-owner retry fencing to pursue tenant fairness while controlling duplicate retry decisions across replicas.
And what remains unproven by stating that design?

The proposal alone does not show that each tenant receives at least 90% of its weighted fair throughput under feasible demand, or that attempts per request stay below 1.2 during backend failures and five-second telemetry delays. It identifies the controls to use, while their detailed rules and measured outcomes remain unspecified.
Can partition-stable reservations maintain at least 90% tenant fair-share attainment when tenant demand shifts unevenly across isolated balancers?

That is an open question. A reservation remaining stable through a partition does not, by itself, show that capacity is available where a tenant’s demand appears. The issue is whether each tenant can still receive at least 90% of its weighted fair throughput when its demand is unevenly distributed among balancers that cannot coordinate. No attainment result for that condition is stated.
What does “partition-stable” guarantee in the question?

It describes the intended stability of tenant capacity reservations while balancers are isolated. It does not specify the reservation amounts, where reserved capacity resides, or how reservations respond to demand shifts. Stability of an allocation and sufficient delivered service are different claims.
If the reservations remain intact, why might fair-share attainment still fall?

A tenant could have demand at one isolated balancer while some capacity associated with its reservation is available elsewhere. Without a specified way to use that capacity across the partition, preserving the reservation’s accounting would not necessarily deliver service where it is needed. That is a conceptual possibility, not an observed shortfall.
Are we saying capacity definitely gets stranded?

No. The question does not report stranded capacity or identify a cause. It asks whether reservations can maintain the fair-share bound despite uneven demand across isolated balancers. Whether capacity remains usable depends on allocation and borrowing behavior that has not been specified.
Could local borrowing resolve the uneven-demand problem?

It might help a balancer use capacity that would otherwise be idle locally. But local borrowing does not, on its own, establish that capacity needed by a tenant at one isolated balancer is available there. The proposal names local borrowing without specifying when it is allowed or how a reservation is protected when demand shifts.
Would it be enough for each balancer to honor its own tenant reservations?

Not necessarily. Local compliance says something about each balancer’s allocation decisions; the question concerns each tenant’s resulting fair-share attainment across the isolated balancers. A tenant’s demand and its reserved capacity might not be distributed in matching proportions. No local-to-global guarantee is given.
Should the 90% be checked separately at every balancer?

The stated fairness objective is per tenant, relative to that tenant’s weighted fair throughput under feasible demand.
